records.our_prose: St. George grows fava beans on a single spring, direct-sown cycle, per USU Extension's "Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah," which sets Feb 15 as the St. George Group A (hardy) date, the same slot the table gives peas. Fava beans are named by analogy rather than a dedicated table line, but their own cold tolerance to about 12°F fits that early date well. Pods begin filling about 90 days later and the crop is harvested by late May, well before St. George reaches 100°F in June, July, and August. USU documents no fall planting date for fava beans, so the bed rests through the hot months rather than carrying a second cycle.

records.our_prose: Fava beans do best on a well-drained silt loam or loam with compost worked in, but they are adaptable and tolerate clay, loam, and sand, and they are salt tolerant once established. Good drainage is the priority: the big flat seeds are slow to germinate in cool soil and rot readily if sown into cold, saturated ground. As a legume, fava fixes much of its own nitrogen through root nodules, so the bed needs tilth and fertility more than heavy feeding. Because favas are often used as a cover crop and green manure, they in turn leave the soil looser and richer for what follows.

records.source_context: Grown primarily for its nutritious seeds and pods which are high in protein and consumed by millions of people throughout the world. Legumes also have the ability to fix nitrogen from the air and are often used as a cover crop. It is a stiffly erect plant that grows 2-6 feet tall and prefers moist loams but is tolerant of clay and saline soils and once established, drought.

records.our_prose: Direct-sow the large flat seed about 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart, thinning to stand 8 to 10 inches apart, in rows 18 to 30 inches apart. Germination is slow in cool soil and can take up to three weeks; there is no benefit to starting favas indoors.

records.our_prose: Unlike peas, favas stand up on their own sturdy stalks and do not need a trellis. Tall types can lean over in wind or rain, so put a stake at each end of the row and run string down both sides to hold them up. Keep the plants from crowding so air moves through and disease stays down.
